A lot of parents are quietly confused about the same thing. Their kid works as hard as anyone on the roster and still sits more than they play.
It almost never comes down to effort. Coaches put the game in the hands of players they trust, and trust gets earned in the moments that decide possession. The ball arrives, there's a defender closing, and the player has a half-second to settle it and pick the right next move. Do that consistently and a coach relaxes. Cough it up under pressure a few times and they reach for someone else.
That's the part most training never touches. Pickup games and big group sessions don't slow down enough to fix what happens in that half-second.
When a player gets coached on it, the change shows up where it counts. The first touch settles instead of skipping away. They keep the ball when it's tight, which earns a coach's trust, which turns into longer runs on the field, which turns into the kind of games that move a kid up the depth chart instead of down it.
That's what the 8-week summer program at SMAA is built around. Small groups, so every athlete actually gets coached on their touch and their decisions, not just run through drills. It opens with a free 1:1 evaluation where Coach Jeremy (MS, CSCS, 10 years coaching) pinpoints what's keeping your player off the field and how to fix it.
If they don't show real progress in the first month, training continues free until they do. That's the SMAA promise.

Why effort doesn't earn minutes

If you've got a kid who works hard and still doesn't play much, you already know how confusing it is from the sideline. They hustle in practice. They do everything the coach asks. And then the whistle blows and they're watching.
The hard part to hear is that effort isn't what earns minutes. Coaches give the game to the players they trust when it's tight, and trust is built somewhere most people never look. It's the half-second after the ball arrives, with a defender bearing down, when the player has to settle it and make the right next move. Handle that moment well, again and again, and the coach stops thinking twice about leaving them in. Lose the ball there a few times in a close game, and the next sub is already warming up.
Almost no normal training touches that moment. Pickup games are too chaotic. Big group sessions move too fast to fix one player's first touch. So the kid keeps working hard on everything except the exact thing that's costing them the field.
When that gets coached, here's how it actually plays out. The first touch starts to settle instead of bouncing loose. The player keeps the ball under pressure instead of giving it back, which means the coach trusts them with it a little longer, which means more time on the field, which means more chances to make a play a coach remembers, and a few of those is how a kid climbs the depth chart instead of sliding down it.
That's the whole point of the 8-week summer program at SMAA. The groups are small on purpose, so every athlete gets real coaching on their touch, their scanning, and their decisions every session, not just laps and lines. It opens with a free 1:1 evaluation, a 45-minute session where Coach Jeremy (MS, CSCS, 10 years coaching, former college player) runs your child through a hands-on assessment and shows you exactly what's keeping them off the field and what to do about it.
And SMAA stands behind the work. If your player doesn't feel more confident, sharpen their game, or show real progress after the first month, training continues free until they do.

ad-b1.headline.text: Why summer makes or breaks players

ad-b1.primaryText.text:
Most young soccer players don't get better over the summer. They just stay busy.
Pickup games, a camp here and there, the same drills in the backyard. It fills the calendar. It doesn't move the needle on first touch, first step, or how they hold up in the second half.

ad-b3.headline.text: Why a busy summer isn't enough

ad-b3.primaryText.text:
Most young soccer players will spend this summer playing a lot of soccer and getting almost no better at it.
That sounds harsh, so let me be clear about what I mean. The effort isn't the issue. These kids work. They play pickup, they go to a camp, they juggle in the driveway. What's missing is anyone watching closely enough to catch the small things, the first touch that's a half-second slow, the plant foot that's in the wrong spot, the body that's square when it should be open. Without that, every rep just reinforces what they already do.
Summer is the worst possible time to let that ride. There are no games to win and no standings to chase, which is exactly why it's the window where players separate. The kids who get coached on the details come back in the fall looking like a different player. The kids who just stayed busy come back the same, a step behind kids who weren't even more talented in June.
Here's how the separation actually plays out. A cleaner first touch means the ball sticks under pressure instead of skipping away. Keeping the ball means more touches every single game. More touches means more chances to do something with it, and that builds the composure a coach can see from the sideline. Composure on the ball is what earns trust, trust is what turns into real minutes, and the player who's getting minutes in the fall is the one who spent the summer getting coached instead of just getting tired.

ad-c2.headline.text: When a kid stops asking for the ball

ad-c2.primaryText.text:
Most parents notice it before they can name it. Their kid used to chase the ball everywhere. Now they drift to the edges and hope it goes to someone else.
It looks like a confidence problem, and everyone treats it like one. More encouragement, more pep talks in the car, more reminding them how good they are. It rarely moves anything, because confidence on the field was never the starting point. It's the result.
A player who isn't sure they can control the ball under pressure will avoid it. That's not nerves. That's a skill gap wearing a confidence mask. Fix the touch and the avoidance goes with it.
You can actually watch the order it happens in. The first touch starts to settle, so the fear of losing the ball fades, so the player stops hiding and starts asking for it again, so they get more involved, and the more involved they are the more those small wins stack into the belief no pep talk could give them.

ad-c3.primaryText.text:
If your kid has gone quiet on the field lately, you already know the feeling from the sideline. You watch them pull back after a bad touch. You see them stop calling for the ball. And you'd give anything to reach out there and remind them how good they actually are.
The hard truth is that confidence can't be handed to a player from the outside. You can't pep-talk it in, and you can't love it into them either, as much as every parent wishes they could. Belief on the field is built in one direction only. A kid has to feel, in their own feet, that they can handle the ball when it matters. The skill comes first. The confidence is what grows out of it.
So when a player goes quiet, it's almost never a character thing. It's usually that one part of their game stopped feeling reliable, the first touch under pressure, and their body started protecting them from the moment that keeps going wrong. Drifting to the edges isn't shyness. It's self-protection. And no amount of encouragement fixes a skill gap, because encouragement was never the missing piece.
Here's the part that's actually hopeful, because you can watch it happen in order. When the touch gets coached and starts to settle, the fear of losing the ball quiets down. When that fear quiets, the player stops hiding and starts asking for the ball again. The more they get on it, the more small wins they collect, and those small wins stack into the kind of steady belief that shows up as a kid playing free instead of playing scared.
That's the whole point of the 8-week summer program at SMAA. The groups stay small on purpose, so every athlete gets real coaching on the skill underneath their confidence, every session, not just a "good job" from the sideline. It opens with a free 1:1 evaluation, a 45-minute session where Coach Jeremy (MS, CSCS, 10 years coaching, former college player) runs your child through a hands-on assessment and shows you exactly where their belief is getting stuck and how to rebuild it from the skill up.
And SMAA stands behind it. If your child doesn't feel more confident, sharpen their skills, or show real progress after the first month, training continues free until they do.
The timing is on your side here. We're opening our Saco location on June 8, and the first group of families in comes on as founding members: $100 off the summer program, with the opening cohort capped so every athlete is coached from day one. These 8 weeks happen either way. A kid who spends them quietly building real skill walks into fall games willing to ask for the ball again. A kid who spends them waiting for the confidence to just come back usually walks in the same way they left.

-Coach Jeremy
